👩🏻‍💻 What should you look for when searching for a new team as a junior dev?

➡️ Whether you’re applying to a new company or looking to join a different team at your current company, team fit is extremely important, especially when you’re just starting out in your career. Here are some things to look out for:

🌙 A technical lead that is invested in the growth of the team – no matter how ‘smart’ or experienced your teammates are, a tech lead will push everyone to grow. Not only will they help you with bugs and review your code, but they’ll also guide you through the systems and code bases at your company.

🌙 A manager that has experience managing junior developers (may or may not also be your tech lead) – they know exactly what you need to develop your professional and coding skills to the next level and how to help you succeed at the company. They are especially attentive to concerns that junior developers may have such as developing their voice, career growth, and supplemental trainings.

🌙 A team you enjoy talking to – contrary to popular belief, engineers work very collaboratively and there’s a lot of time to talk between code reviews, waiting for CI, and just hanging out together every day. You don’t need to work with your best friends (and you probably won’t!), but you should at least enjoy talking to them about tv, sports, tech etc.

🌙 Diversity - diversity itself can be defined in your own terms, but diversity is important to junior developers because it can lead to an inclusive team that values your opinion, even as a junior dev! Diversity isn’t just gender diversity. It’s also diversity of age, ability, experience, and so much more. Having a diverse team leads to effective ideation, better products, members feeling included and valued at work and ultimately helps with imposter syndrome. Also: individuals are not diverse, groups of people are!

❓ What do you look for when searching for a new team?

👩🏻‍💻 What even is CI?

⌨️ Continuous integration (CI) is a DevOps practice where engineers regularly push their code into a shared repository. Each time new code is pushed, the automated integration pipeline checks to see if the code compiled successfully, it runs tests and linters, and bundles all of the code. If anything does fail, the engineer is notified automatically so they can fix it asap!

🖥 CI (and CD) is often modified by companies to match their engineering cultures, so it may not look the same in practice. BUT the principles of the theory are still true across the board:

🌟 Find and fix bugs immediately

🌟 Ensure software quality

🌟 Automate tests

🌟 Deliver features to customers quickly

💪🏼 Did you know that coding and lifting weights have a lot in common? Here are a few reasons why I (mostly) love both:

👩🏻‍💻 They teach you RESILIENCE. When you start lifting and coding, you don’t know what you’re doing. You constantly look online to double check and it all just feels so uncomfortable. But that’s okay! Day by day, you’ll get stronger and more comfortable with coding. If you think you’ve hit a plateau, look back and appreciate the physical and mental progress you’ve made.

 🏋🏻‍♀️ Form MATTERS. Whether it’s clean code or correct form when performing an exercise, your success depends on form. Yes, you *can* progress with bad form, but eventually it’ll catch up to you. An injury will keep you away from the gym and bad coding styles will prevent you from getting a job. Both are painful.

👥 They are historically BOYS clubs. The unfortunate fact is that many women (including myself) are/were intimidated by the number of males in the tech industry and in the weight room. They say we can’t make it or that we’ll get too ‘bulky’ so we shy away from engineering roles and stick to the cardio machines.

💅🏼 BUT the communities of strong women who code and strong women who lift are SO SO supportive. There is so much knowledge passed down from woman to woman and we love to cheer each other on, whether it’s hitting a new PR or getting a promotion! Plus, we look good doing it 😉

🖥 People on the internet will always think they know more than you (and tell you that you’re wrong). Usually, they give you some pretty bad advice simply because they think they are ‘better’. You know where you are on your journey and don’t let unsolicited ‘advice’ get to you. Your progress is YOUR progress.

❓What other similarities can you think of?

🌟 Let’s talk about end of year assessments!

👩🏻‍💻 It’s crucial to plan out what you’re going to write in your annual self assessment. Your reviews are used to determine your bonus, potential promotions, and even shifts to a management role. It’s not just something you have to get done in order to get back to your sprint work–it directly impacts your career and financial goals!

📓 To help me write the best self review, I have a list of all my achievements and projects in the past year. I jot down moments (as they happen) where I showed leadership and/or technical expertise such as spearheading a new project or solving a complicated bug. I also include ‘company culture’ related activities, including volunteering with the company and organizing events for the Employee Resource Groups.

👥 Don’t forget to name drop coworkers that you worked with in your review! Coding professionally is extremely collaborative and your managers will most likely be asking others about your performance. Pointing them to individuals who can give more insightful feedback will only benefit your review.
